# Introduction

While an ADaM dataset is being derived it is easy to lose track of what it
contains: did `derive_param_computed()` add the parameter you expected, is the
correct number of flags present in the dataset, is there still only one
baseline record per subject and parameter?

`{admiral}` helps answer these questions with the `admiral_df` class. A dataset
of this class can carry a little metadata about itself -- its name, its ADaM
class, and its key variables -- and calling [`summary()`](../reference/summary.admiral_df.html) on it prints a short
report tailored to the kind of dataset it is, including some sanity checks.

This article shows how to:

- Tag a dataset with `admiral_df()` and read its metadata back,
- Use `summary()` to inspect a dataset *in flight*, i.e. at any point of a
  derivation pipeline,
- Keep the class and metadata when using `{dplyr}` and `{tidyr}`, as some
  common operations keep them, some keep them only in part, and some drop them.

**Note**: The `admiral_df` class and the functions described here are
[experimental](https://pharmaverse.github.io/admiraldev/articles/programming_strategy.html#experimental-functions),
so their behavior may still change.

## Required Packages

The examples in this article use the following packages and the example ADSL
and ADLB datasets which come with `{admiral}`. Both datasets are already tagged
with their metadata, as described below.

```{r message=FALSE}
library(admiral)
library(dplyr, warn.conflicts = FALSE)
library(tibble)

adsl <- admiral_adsl
adlb <- admiral_adlb
```

# What is an `admiral_df`?

An `admiral_df` is an ordinary data frame (usually a tibble) with an extra
class. Everything you can do with a tibble you can still do with an
`admiral_df`; it only changes how the dataset is printed and summarized.

All `{admiral}` functions which create or modify a dataset, such as the
`derive_*()` functions, return an `admiral_df`. So as soon as a dataset has
passed through an `{admiral}` function, `summary()` gives the `{admiral}`
report rather than the base R one.

```{r}
adsl <- derive_vars_dt(
  adsl,
  new_vars_prefix = "RFST",
  dtc = RFSTDTC
)

class(adsl)
```

In addition, a dataset can store three pieces of metadata:

| Metadata    | Example                               | Read back with        |
|-------------|---------------------------------------|-----------------------|
| Name        | `"ADLB"`                              | `get_dataset_name()`  |
| ADaM class  | `"BDS"`                               | `get_dataset_class()` |
| Key variables | `exprs(USUBJID, PARAMCD, AVISIT)`   | `get_dataset_keys()`  |

The key variables are the variables which together should uniquely identify
each record of the dataset. They are what `summary()` checks the record
structure against.

# Tagging a Dataset

The metadata is set with `admiral_df()`. Any data frame can be passed to it,
whether or not it has the `admiral_df` class yet.

```{r}
adlb <- admiral_df(
  adlb,
  dataset_name = "ADLB",
  dataset_class = "BDS",
  dataset_keys = exprs(STUDYID, USUBJID, PARAMCD, AVISIT)
)
```

When the metadata has been set, it is shown in a header line when the dataset
is printed:

```{r}
adlb %>%
  select(USUBJID, PARAMCD, AVISIT, AVAL) %>%
  head(3)
```

and it can be read back with the `get_*()` functions listed in the table above.
`get_dataset_keys()` returns a list of symbols, so the keys can be passed
straight to a `by_vars` argument of another function:

```{r}
get_dataset_keys(adlb)
```

## Updating the Metadata

Calling `admiral_df()` again on a dataset which already has metadata updates
only the items which are supplied. Anything left as `NULL` is kept:

```{r}
adlb <- admiral_df(adlb, dataset_keys = exprs(STUDYID, USUBJID, PARAMCD, ADT, DTYPE))

get_dataset_name(adlb)
get_dataset_keys(adlb)
```

If one of the keys is not a variable of the dataset, perhaps because of a
typo, a warning is issued and the keys are left as they were:

```{r}
adlb_typo <- admiral_df(adlb, dataset_keys = exprs(USUBJID, PARAMDC))
```

To record that a dataset has no key variables at all, pass an empty list,
`exprs()`. This is different from never setting the keys.

## Where do the Keys Come From?

`{admiral}` never guesses the keys of a dataset. They can come from your
dataset specification, from the `by_vars` of the derivation which created the
dataset, or simply be written by hand. A specification usually provides them
as a character vector, which `chr2vars()` converts. For example, with a
`{metacore}` specification:

```{r eval=FALSE}
adlb <- admiral_df(
  adlb,
  dataset_keys = chr2vars(metacore::get_keys(spec, "ADLB")$variable),
  dataset_name = "ADLB"
)
```

## The ADaM Class

The ADaM class decides what `summary()` reports. The supported classes are
`"ADSL"`, `"BDS"`, `"OCCDS"`, and `"TTE"`, and for medical device data
`"ADDL"`, `"MDBDS"`, `"MDOCCDS"`, and `"MDTTE"`.

Unlike the keys, the class does not have to be set: if it has not been,
`{admiral}` does its best to infer it from the variables and records of the
dataset. For example, a dataset with `PARAMCD` and `AVAL` is inferred as
`"BDS"`, one with occurrence variables such as `AEDECOD` or `TRTEMFL` as
`"OCCDS"`, and one with neither and one record per subject as `"ADSL"`:

```{r}
adae <- tribble(
  ~STUDYID,  ~USUBJID,      ~AEDECOD,
  "PILOT01", "01-701-1015", "HEADACHE",
  "PILOT01", "01-701-1023", "NAUSEA"
)

get_dataset_class(adae)
```

When printed, an inferred class is marked as such. If the inferred class is
wrong for your dataset -- for example an ADAE which has been restricted to
device related events may be taken for device data -- set it with
`admiral_df()`. A class that has been set always takes precedence.

# Summarizing a Dataset in Flight

Calling `summary()` on an `admiral_df` prints a report on the dataset. It
always shows the name and ADaM class, the number of subjects, records and
variables, and whether there is one record per key. Depending on the ADaM class
it then adds:

- **ADSL**: subjects per treatment arm, population flags, subject flow
  (randomized, treated, completed), treatment duration, end of study status,
  deaths and their causes, and age and sex.
- **BDS**: the records, subjects and visits of each parameter, with the
  distribution of `AVAL` for numeric parameters and the distinct `AVALC` values
  for character ones, the analysis visits, the derived records per `DTYPE`, and
  checks that every parameter has `AVAL` or `AVALC` populated and that there is
  at most one baseline record (`ABLFL`) per subject, parameter, and `BASETYPE`.
- **OCCDS**: the number of distinct terms, treatment-emergent and serious
  records, records per severity and per toxicity grade, and a check that each
  occurrence flag (`AOCCFL`, `AOCCPFL`, ...) has at most one `"Y"` per group.
- **TTE**: events and censored records per parameter.

```{r}
summary(adsl)
```

```{r}
summary(adlb)
```

Each item is only reported when the variables it needs are in the dataset. So
`summary()` can be called at any point of a derivation: a dataset which is only
half derived gives a shorter report, not an error.

## Checking the Record Structure

The structure line compares the records with the keys:

- `✔` -- there is one record per combination of the keys,
- `✖` -- some combinations have more than one record, and how many extra
  records there are,
- `ℹ` -- no keys have been set, so the structure was not checked,
- `!` -- some keys are no longer variables of the dataset (e.g. after a
  `select()` or `rename()`), so the structure was not checked.

For example, imagine a merge accidentally duplicated some records. Without
looking through the data, `summary()` reports it straight away:

```{r}
adlb_dup <- bind_rows(adlb, slice(adlb, 1:2))

summary(adlb_dup)
```

## Comparing with ADSL

A dataset cannot tell by itself which subjects are missing from it. If ADSL is
passed to the `adsl` argument, `summary()` also reports how many of the ADSL
subjects have records -- overall, in the safety population, and per treatment
arm -- and checks that every subject in the dataset is in ADSL. For an OCCDS
dataset it also reports the subjects with a treatment-emergent record.

```{r}
summary(adlb, adsl = adsl)
```

## A Worked Example

Summaries are most useful straight after a derivation, to confirm it did what
you expected. Here we add a parameter for the ratio of ALT to AST:

```{r}
adlb_ratio <- adlb %>%
  derive_param_computed(
    by_vars = exprs(STUDYID, USUBJID, AVISIT, AVISITN, ADT),
    parameters = c("ALT", "AST"),
    set_values_to = exprs(
      AVAL = AVAL.ALT / AVAL.AST,
      PARAMCD = "ALTAST",
      PARAM = "ALT/AST Ratio"
    )
  )

summary(adlb_ratio)
```

The derivation ran without an error or a warning, but the summary shows that
something went wrong: the structure check finds 26 extra records. The ratio was
also computed for the derived `"POST-BASELINE"` visits (`DTYPE` is `"LOV"`,
`"MAXIMUM"`, or `"MINIMUM"`). As `DTYPE` is not set for the new records, these
duplicate the ratio of the observed visit on the same date.

The fix is to compute the ratio from the observed records only. The `filter`
argument of `derive_param_computed()` does this without dropping the derived
records from the dataset, as filtering the dataset beforehand would:

```{r}
adlb_ratio <- adlb %>%
  derive_param_computed(
    by_vars = exprs(STUDYID, USUBJID, AVISIT, AVISITN, ADT),
    filter = is.na(DTYPE),
    parameters = c("ALT", "AST"),
    set_values_to = exprs(
      AVAL = AVAL.ALT / AVAL.AST,
      PARAMCD = "ALTAST",
      PARAM = "ALT/AST Ratio"
    )
  )

summary(adlb_ratio)
```

Now the structure check passes, and `ALTAST` has a record for each observed
visit with both values.

## Using the Summary Programmatically

`summary()` returns a list, which is printed. Its elements can be used in your
own checks, e.g. to warn, or stop a program, if the record structure is wrong:

```{r}
smry <- summary(adlb_dup)

smry$structure$n_duplicates

if (isTRUE(smry$structure$n_duplicates > 0)) {
  cli::cli_warn("Duplicates detected!")
}
```

`n_duplicates` is `NA` if the structure was not checked, e.g. because no keys
were set, hence the `isTRUE()`.

# What Happens to the Class and Metadata?

The class and metadata are stored as attributes of the data frame. Whether they
survive an operation depends on whether it modifies the existing data frame or
builds a new one. The table below summarizes what common operations do to an
`admiral_df` with metadata set.

```{r echo=FALSE}
ops <- tribble(
  ~Operation, ~Class, ~Metadata,
  "`mutate()`, `filter()`, `arrange()`, `slice()`, `relocate()`, `head()`", "kept", "kept",
  "`mutate(.by = )`, `filter(.by = )`", "kept", "kept",
  "`left_join()` etc. and `semi_join()`/`anti_join()`, dataset as `x`", "kept", "kept",
  "`bind_rows()`, dataset as *first* argument; `rbind()`", "kept", "kept",
  "`select()`, `rename()`, `transmute()`, `distinct()`, `count()`", "kept", "kept, may be out of date",
  "`group_by()`, `rowwise()`", "dropped", "kept",
  "`as_tibble()`, `as.data.frame()`", "dropped", "kept",
  "`group_by()` ... `ungroup()`, `rowwise()` ... `ungroup()`", "dropped", "dropped",
  "`summarise()`, `reframe()`", "dropped", "dropped",
  "`left_join()` etc., dataset as `y`", "dropped", "dropped",
  "`bind_rows()`, dataset *not* the first argument", "dropped", "dropped",
  "`tidyr::pivot_longer()`, `pivot_wider()`, `complete()`, `nest()`/`unnest()`", "dropped", "dropped",
  "`{admiral}` functions, e.g. `derive_var_extreme_flag()`", "kept", "not guaranteed"
)
knitr::kable(ops)
```

## Kept

Operations which change the values or the order of the records, but keep the
data frame they were given, keep everything. This covers most of the code in a
typical ADaM script:

```{r}
adlb %>%
  filter(PARAMCD == "ALT") %>%
  mutate(AVALCAT1 = if_else(AVAL > 40, "> 40", "<= 40")) %>%
  get_dataset_name()
```

Joins and `bind_rows()` keep the attributes of the dataset which comes *first*.
If the dataset with the metadata is the `x` of a join, or the first dataset of
`bind_rows()`, everything is kept; otherwise the metadata of the other dataset
is used, which usually means none.

```{r}
# ADLB is `x`: kept
left_join(adlb, select(adsl, STUDYID, USUBJID, RFSTDT), by = c("STUDYID", "USUBJID")) %>%
  get_dataset_name()

# ADLB is `y`: dropped
left_join(select(adsl, STUDYID, USUBJID), adlb, by = c("STUDYID", "USUBJID")) %>%
  get_dataset_name()
```

## Partially Kept

### Metadata kept, but possibly out of date

`select()`, `rename()`, `transmute()`, `distinct()`, and `count()` keep the
class and metadata, but they change the variables, so the stored keys may no
longer match the dataset. The keys are stored as plain names, so they are not
renamed along with the variables. `summary()` tells you when this has happened:

```{r}
adlb %>%
  rename(SUBJECT = USUBJID) %>%
  summary()
```

Similarly, `count()` and `distinct()` return a dataset which keeps the name and
class of the original, even though it is no longer an ADLB. Bear this in mind
when printing or summarizing their results.

### Metadata kept, class dropped

`group_by()` and `rowwise()` return a grouped data frame, and `as_tibble()` and
`as.data.frame()` return a plain one. They keep the metadata, but not the
`admiral_df` class, so `print()` and `summary()` fall back to their usual
behavior. The metadata is still there, so calling `admiral_df()` without any
other arguments restores the class together with it:

```{r}
adlb_tbl <- as_tibble(adlb)

class(adlb_tbl)

adlb_tbl %>%
  admiral_df() %>%
  get_dataset_name()
```

### `{admiral}` functions

All `{admiral}` functions return an `admiral_df`, so the class is always kept.
The metadata, however, is not guaranteed to be: functions which build their
result from a grouped or summarized dataset internally lose it, while others
keep it. For example, `derive_var_extreme_flag()` drops it:

```{r}
adlb %>%
  filter(is.na(DTYPE)) %>%
  derive_var_extreme_flag(
    by_vars = exprs(STUDYID, USUBJID, PARAMCD),
    order = exprs(ADT),
    new_var = LASTFL,
    mode = "last"
  ) %>%
  get_dataset_name()
```

## Dropped

`summarise()`, the `{tidyr}` reshaping functions, and the grouped pipelines
which end in `ungroup()` build a new data frame, which has neither the class
nor the metadata. Note that `group_by()` followed by `ungroup()` drops
everything, even though `group_by()` on its own keeps the metadata:

```{r}
adlb %>%
  group_by(USUBJID, PARAMCD) %>%
  mutate(N_VISITS = n()) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  class()
```

Where possible, use the `.by` argument instead, which keeps everything:

```{r}
adlb %>%
  mutate(N_VISITS = n(), .by = c(USUBJID, PARAMCD)) %>%
  get_dataset_name()
```

Otherwise, call `admiral_df()` again with the metadata after the operation.

# Recommendations

- **Tag the dataset late.** As the metadata may be lost during a derivation,
  call `admiral_df()` once the dataset is (nearly) finished, or just before you
  want to summarize it, rather than at the start of the script.
- **Re-tag after operations which drop it.** If you need the summary in the
  middle of a pipeline, call `admiral_df()` again with the metadata. Keeping the
  keys in a variable, e.g. `adlb_keys <- exprs(STUDYID, USUBJID, PARAMCD,
  AVISIT)`, makes this easy.
- **Remove grouping first.** `admiral_df()` does not accept grouped datasets, so call
  `ungroup()` before it.
- **Summarize after each important derivation.** Comparing the summaries
  before and after a derivation is a quick way to see exactly what it added or
  changed.
- **Pass ADSL** to `summary()` to see the subjects which have no records, or
  should not be in the dataset.
